usage: 여자친구가 또 토라졌어요.
My girlfriend got in a huff again.
Classic relationship word — a partner gets quietly upset and goes cold.
사소한 일에 토라지지 마.
Don't sulk over little things.
친구·연인 사이 반말. The 'turn away and go silent' nuance is built in.
토라져서 등을 홱 돌렸어요.
She sulked and turned her back sharply.
토라지다 habitually pairs with 등을 돌리다 (turn one's back) — the physical 'turning away' is the heart of the word.
삐친 게 아니라 단단히 토라졌어.
It's not a light huff — she's properly sulking.
단단히 토라지다 = sulk hard/seriously, a step beyond casual 삐치다.
examples: 내가 농담한 걸 갖고 하루 종일 토라져 있었어.
She sulked all day over a joke I made.
토라져 있다 = staying in the sulking state for a stretch of time.
뭐 때문에 토라진 거야? 말을 해 줘야 알지.
What are you sulking about? You have to tell me so I know.
A very natural thing to say to a sulking partner; 토라진 거야 reads the sulk as ongoing.
선물 받고 금방 기분이 풀려서 더 이상 안 토라졌어요.
She got a gift and cheered up, so she stopped sulking.
기분이 풀리다 = the mood un-knots; the natural exit from 토라지다.
nuance: 토라지다 is the specific sulk where someone feels hurt or slighted and pointedly turns cold — going quiet, looking away, giving you the silent treatment. The dividing line versus its near-synonym 삐치다 matters: 삐치다 just names the hurt-and-pouty feeling, while 토라지다 foregrounds the visible turning-away and icy withdrawal, so it sounds a touch more serious and dramatic (단단히 토라지다 = sulk hard). It is far softer and more passive than 화내다, where the person openly shouts; a person who 토라지다 withdraws rather than explodes. Register is casual and affectionate, used overwhelmingly of couples, close friends, and children — you would not say a CEO 토라졌다 in a formal report. It collocates with 등을 돌리다, 입을 삐죽 내밀다, and the recovery phrase 기분이 풀리다. English-speaker pitfall: do not reach for 'angry' and translate it as 화나다 — that loses the whole 'silent, turned-away' core; also resist adding an object with 을/를, because 토라지다 is intransitive (you 토라지다 at a state, you don't 토라지다 something).

Past tense is 토라졌어요 (토라지 + 었 → 토라졌). Don't spell it 토라젔어요 or 토라졌써요.

english: to get in a huff (and sulk)
usage: 야, 삐쳤어?
Hey, are you upset (with me)?
The single most common way to ask if a friend is sulking. Casual 반말.
그런 걸로 삐치지 마세요.
Don't get all huffy over something like that.
Gently telling someone they're overreacting and sulking — softened to 존댓말.
삐친 척하지 마.
Don't pretend to be sulking.
삐친 척 = the act of sulking; couples tease each other with fake huffs.
나 삐쳤거든? 풀어 줘.
I'm sulking, you know? Make it up to me.
풀어 주다 = un-knot someone's huff; the playful flip side of 삐치다.
examples: 내가 답장 늦게 했다고 삐쳤어.
He got in a huff because I replied late.
Texting culture — late replies genuinely make people 삐치다; -다고 gives the reason.
삐친 거 아니야? 목소리가 왜 그래?
Aren't you sulking? Why do you sound like that?
Reading a sulky tone in someone's voice.
금방 삐치고 금방 풀리는 성격이에요.
He gets in a huff easily and gets over it just as fast.
Describing a personality that sulks quickly but holds no grudge; 풀리다 = the huff dissolves.
nuance: 삐치다 (very commonly spoken and spelled 삐지다) is the everyday word for getting into a sulky huff because your feelings were nicked — someone forgot you, replied late, left you out, or made a joke at your expense. The boundary versus 토라지다 is one of emphasis: 삐치다 spotlights the hurt-and-pouty internal state and is lighter, cuter, more childish, whereas 토라지다 adds the cold turning-away. It is far gentler than 화내다 (real anger) and is used constantly and affectionately among friends, siblings, and couples, often half-joking ('너 삐쳤어?'). It collocates with 금방 (삐쳤다 풀렸다 = huffed then got over it), the recovery verb 풀리다/풀어 주다, and 삐친 척 (pretend-sulking). English-speaker pitfall: learners overreach and translate any 'annoyed/angry' as 삐치다 — but 삐치다 is specifically the wounded-feelings pout, not general irritation (that's 짜증나다) and not shouting (that's 화내다). Also note it is intransitive: 나한테 삐쳤어, not 나를 삐쳤어.

mistakes: 삐지다 is the very common spoken variant; both are widely understood, but 삐치다 is the standard dictionary form, so prefer it in writing.
It's intransitive — say 친구가 삐쳤어요 / 나한테 삐쳤어요, never 친구를 삐쳤어요.
Past tense is 삐쳤어요 (삐치 + 었 → 삐쳐 + ㅆ). Don't write it as 삐쳣어요 or 삐쳤써요.

usage: 그만 좀 골내!
Quit being sulky and grumpy!
Reads as 'stop brooding in a sour mood'. Casual command.
애도 아니고 그런 걸로 골내요?
You're not a kid — are you really getting grumpy over that?
Calling out childish moodiness; 애도 아니고 = 'you're not even a child'.
골난 표정 좀 풀어.
Lighten up that grumpy face.
골난 표정 = a sullen look; 풀다 = release/un-knot the mood.
괜히 나한테 골내지 마.
Don't take your grumpy mood out on me for no reason.
한테 marks the target; 괜히 = needlessly.
examples: 게임에서 졌다고 혼자 골내고 있어.
He's off by himself sulking because he lost the game.
골내다 = a moody, irritated sulk; pairs with 혼자 (alone).
동생이 골낸 표정으로 방에 들어가 버렸어요.
My younger sibling went into the room with a grumpy face.
골낸 표정 = a sullen, sulky expression; -아/어 버리다 adds the 'stormed off' feel.
사소한 일로 골내지 말고 그냥 얘기해.
Don't get all grumpy over a small thing — just talk it out.
Encouraging communication instead of brooding.
nuance: 골내다 blends sulking with irritation — a grumpy, moody upset where someone broods, gives off a sour mood, and goes half-pouting, half-cross. On the spectrum it sits between 삐치다 (lighter, just hurt feelings) and 화내다 (open anger): grumpier and more visibly cross than 삐치다, but not the explosive shouting of 화내다. The word is built like 화내다: the noun 골 here means 'temper/sour mood' (as in 골이 났다 / 골이 잔뜩 났다), and 내다 means 'to put out/express', so 골내다 literally = 'to put out a sour temper'. Its intransitive partner is 골나다 ('to become grumpy'), exactly mirroring 화내다 / 화나다. It collocates with 혼자 (sulking alone), 골난 표정 (a sullen face), and ...한테 골내다 (be grumpy at someone). English-speaker pitfall: keep the 내다/나다 split straight — you 골내다 (actively show it) but you 골나다 (the mood arises in you); and don't confuse this 골 (temper) with the homographs 골 meaning 'brain' or the loanword 'goal'. It is colloquial, so it stays in casual speech, not formal writing.

Don't confuse this 골 (temper/sour mood) with the homographs 골 ('brain') or the loanword 골 ('goal') — only context tells them apart.
It's colloquial; in formal or written contexts prefer 화내다 or 짜증을 내다 instead of 골내다.

usage: 나한테 짜증내지 마.
Don't take your irritation out on me.
Hugely common. The 'directed at me' meaning comes from 한테.
왜 자꾸 짜증내요?
Why do you keep snapping?
자꾸 (repeatedly) makes it feel like nagging, ongoing irritation.
짜증 섞인 말투로 대답했어요.
He answered in an irritation-laced tone.
짜증 섞이다 = mixed with irritation; a natural noun collocation of 짜증.
사춘기라 그런지 짜증을 자주 내요.
Maybe because of puberty, they get snippy a lot.
Notice 짜증을 내다 — the noun 짜증 can split off and take 을.
examples: 배고프면 나도 모르게 짜증내게 돼요.
When I'm hungry I end up getting irritable without realizing it.
Very relatable; -게 되다 = end up doing.
사장님이 직원들한테 짜증내서 분위기가 안 좋았어.
The boss snapped at the staff, so the mood was bad.
Workplace scene; 한테 marks who the irritation hit, -아/어서 gives the cause.
짜증내지 말고 차분하게 설명해 줄래?
Could you explain calmly instead of getting irritated?
Contrasts 짜증내다 with 차분하다 (calm).
nuance: 짜증내다 is to outwardly express irritation or annoyance — snapping, a sharp tone, an exasperated huff or face. It is one of the most-used emotion verbs in daily Korean life: clearly negative and usually aimed at someone, yet lighter than full-blown 화내다 (real anger). The crucial contrast for learners is the 내다/나다 pair: 짜증나다 names the internal feeling that wells up ('나 짜증 나' = I'm annoyed / it's annoying me), while 짜증내다 names the outward act of taking it out on someone ('나한테 짜증 내지 마' = don't be snippy at me) — same root noun 짜증, different verb of expression vs arising, just like 화내다 / 화나다. It collocates with 한테 (the target), 자꾸 (repeatedly), 짜증 섞인 말투 (an irritated tone), and the noun can detach as 짜증을 내다. English-speaker pitfall: learners say 나 짜증내 to mean 'I'm annoyed', but that wrongly implies you're actively snapping at someone — use 짜증나 for the feeling. Also, the double ㅉ is a tense consonant romanized 'jj', not a plain 'j'.

To name the target, use 한테/에게, not 을/를: 동생한테 짜증냈어 (correct), not 동생을 짜증냈어.

usage: 애가 장난감 사 달라고 떼써요.
The kid is throwing a fit demanding I buy a toy.
The textbook scene for 떼쓰다 — a child's nagging demand; note -아/어 달라고.
떼쓴다고 다 되는 거 아니야.
Throwing a tantrum doesn't get you everything.
Said to a child (or jokingly to an adult acting like one); -ㄴ다고 = 'just because you...'
생떼를 쓰지 마.
Stop making unreasonable demands.
생떼(를) 쓰다 = the intensified noun form; 생- adds 'utterly baseless'.
떼를 써도 소용없어.
Throwing a fit is useless.
Shows the noun 떼 split off with 를; 소용없다 = to be of no use.
examples: 마트에서 과자 사 달라고 바닥에 누워서 떼썼어요.
He lay on the floor at the mart demanding snacks.
떼썼어요 = past (떼쓰 + 었, the ㅡ drops). Very vivid kid behavior.
어른이 돼서까지 떼쓰면 안 되지.
You can't keep throwing tantrums now that you're an adult.
Playfully scolding adult stubbornness; -까지 = 'even to the point of'.
아무리 떼써도 안 되는 건 안 돼.
No matter how much you whine for it, no means no.
Firm boundary-setting language with kids; 아무리 ...아/어도 = no matter how.
nuance: 떼쓰다 is to insistently, unreasonably demand something — the whining, foot-stamping, floor-flopping, won't-take-no-for-an-answer behavior, prototypically a child but also said of adults acting childishly. It is built from the noun 떼 ('an unreasonable demand / a fit') plus 쓰다 ('to use/employ'), so it literally = 'to employ a fit'; the noun can stand alone as 떼를 쓰다, and the intensified 생떼를 쓰다 means an utterly baseless tantrum. Crucially it centers on stubborn demanding, not sadness or quiet sulking — that is the dividing line versus 보채다 (restless fretful whining/urging) and versus 삐치다 (wounded pouting). Conjugation follows the ㅡ-irregular: the stem 쓰- loses its ㅡ before -어, giving 써 / 써요 / 떼썼어요. It collocates almost obligatorily with -아/어 달라고 (떼쓰다) ('demand that something be done'). English-speaker pitfall: never write 떼쓰어요 — the ㅡ must drop to 떼써요; and watch the vowel, it is 떼 (ㅔ), not 때 (ㅐ).

It's 떼쓰다, not 때쓰다 — the first vowel is ㅔ (떼 = a fit / an unreasonable demand), not ㅐ.
떼쓰다 is stubborn demanding, not quiet sulking — don't use it where 삐치다 (hurt pout) or 보채다 (restless fussing) is meant.

usage: 아기가 배고픈지 계속 보채요.
The baby keeps fussing — maybe it's hungry.
The core use: a baby crying and fretting for a need; 계속 = continuously.
그만 좀 보채, 곧 도착해.
Stop pestering me, we'll be there soon.
Said when someone keeps nagging 'are we there yet?'
빨리 해 달라고 보채지 마.
Stop nagging me to do it faster.
-아/어 달라고 보채다 = pester someone to do something for you.
아이가 안아 달라고 보채네요.
The child is fussing to be picked up.
안아 달라고 보채다 — a very common parenting collocation.
examples: 애가 밤새 보채서 한숨도 못 잤어요.
The baby fussed all night so I didn't sleep a wink.
보채다 + 한숨도 못 자다 = a classic exhausted-parent line.
빨리 가자고 옆에서 자꾸 보채니까 정신이 없어.
He keeps pestering me to hurry, so I can't focus.
보채다 of an impatient adult nagging you to rush; -니까 gives the cause.
뭐가 그렇게 급하다고 보채요?
What's so urgent that you keep pestering me?
Pushing back on someone's impatient nagging.
nuance: 보채다 has two everyday senses that share one feel — restless, repeated fussing. First, a baby or young child fretting and crying for a need (hunger, sleep, wanting to be held: 안아 달라고 보채다). Second, a person impatiently pestering or nagging you to hurry up or give them something (빨리 가자고 보채다). The dividing line versus 떼쓰다 is the type of pressure: 떼쓰다 is a stubborn, specific, won't-budge demand ('buy me THAT toy'), whereas 보채다 leans toward restless, antsy whining and urging without a single fixed demand. It is also gentler and more sympathetic than 떼쓰다 — a fussing baby earns pity, a tantruming one earns a scolding. Conjugation: 보채- + 어 contracts (ㅐ + 어 → ㅐ) to 보채 / 보채요, past 보챘어요. It collocates with 밤새 보채다 (fuss all night), 계속/자꾸 보채다, and -아/어 달라고 보채다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 보채어요 — the vowels contract to 보채요; and don't stretch it to mean adult 'anger' — it is fussing/pestering, never shouting.

보채- + 어 contracts (ㅐ + 어 → ㅐ) to 보채 / 보채요, past 보챘어요.
Don't write 보채어요 — the vowels contract to 보채요. And don't stretch it to mean adult 'anger' — it is fussing/pestering, never shouting.

mistakes: 보채 + 어 contracts to 보채 (보채요), past 보챘어요 — don't write 보채어요.
Mostly for babies or impatient pestering; it does not mean adult 'anger' — don't use it where 화내다 or 짜증내다 is meant.
For a stubborn, fixed demand ('I want THAT one'), use 떼쓰다; 보채다 is the looser, restless fussing.

usage: 우는 아이를 달래고 있어요.
I'm soothing the crying child.
The prototypical use — calming a crying kid.
삐친 친구 좀 달래 줘.
Go smooth things over with the friend who's sulking.
달래다 toward a sulking person = win them back, calm them; 좀 softens the request.
화난 손님을 달래는 게 일이에요.
Calming down angry customers is part of the job.
달래다 also = placate/appease an upset person, not just a child.
마음을 달래려고 음악을 들었어요.
I listened to music to soothe my own heart.
마음을 달래다 = comfort your own feelings — a key non-baby sense.
examples: 사탕으로 달래도 울음을 안 그쳤어요.
Even soothing him with candy didn't stop the crying.
달래도 = even though I soothe; pairs with 울음을 그치다 (stop crying).
화난 고객을 달래느라 진땀을 뺐어요.
I broke a sweat trying to calm down the angry customer.
Service-job reality; -느라 = in the course of (an effortful) doing.
속상한 마음을 달래려고 매운 음식을 먹었어요.
I ate spicy food to soothe my upset feelings.
마음을 달래다 = to comfort/soothe one's own heart; -려고 = in order to.
nuance: 달래다 is to soothe, comfort, or placate someone who is crying, upset, or angry — and, importantly, also to calm your own feelings (마음을 달래다 = comfort one's heart). It is the natural counterpart to 울다, 토라지다, 떼쓰다, 화나다: someone gets upset, and you 달래다 them back to calm. The tone is warm and caring. The dividing line versus 위로하다 (to console) is method and scope: 위로하다 consoles mainly with sympathetic words about a loss or sorrow, while 달래다 actively settles a present upset — by holding, coaxing, distracting, or placating — and works on anger and tantrums too, not just grief. Conjugation: 달래- + 어 contracts to 달래 / 달래요, past 달랬어요. It collocates with 우는 아이를 달래다, 화난 고객을 달래다, ...로 달래다 (소리로/사탕으로 달래다 = soothe with...), and 마음을 달래다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 달래어요 — the vowels contract to 달래요; and don't confuse the verb 달래다 with its exact homophone 달래, the wild chive eaten in spring — only context separates them.

달래다 (to soothe, transitive) takes 을/를: 아이를 달래다, 마음을 달래다 — don't drop the object marker.

usage: 등을 토닥여 줬어요.
I gave their back a comforting pat.
토닥이다 + 주다 = pat someone to comfort them; the 주다 shows it's a kindness done for them.
어깨 토닥여 주면서 위로했어요.
I comforted them, patting their shoulder.
Pairs naturally with 위로하다.
아기 재우려고 토닥토닥 해 줬어요.
I patted gently to get the baby to sleep.
The mimetic 토닥토닥 (pat-pat) underlies the verb; 재우다 = put to sleep.
스스로를 토닥여 주는 시간이 필요해요.
You need time to give yourself a comforting pat.
스스로를 토닥이다 = self-comfort, common in self-care talk.
examples: 울지 말라고 아이 등을 토닥여 줬어요.
I patted the child's back, telling them not to cry.
토닥였어요 (past) = 토닥이 + 었; the ㅣ + 어 fuses to 여.
수고했다며 어깨를 토닥여 주셨어요.
He patted my shoulder, saying I'd worked hard.
A very Korean gesture of recognition; -시- marks respect for the senior doing it.
힘든 하루 끝에 스스로를 토닥여 주세요.
At the end of a hard day, give yourself a comforting pat.
스스로를 토닥이다 = self-comfort; gentle imperative with 주세요.
nuance: 토닥이다 is the soft, rhythmic comforting pat — on a back, shoulder, or head — that wordlessly says 'it's okay, you did well.' It is fundamentally a physical act of consolation, almost always paired with 주다 to show you are doing it for someone (등을 토닥여 주다). The word is the verb form of the mimetic adverb 토닥토닥 (the gentle pat-pat sound/motion), which is why it feels so tactile and warm. Its very close companion 다독이다 overlaps heavily, but the dividing line is focus: 토닥이다 stays on the literal, light patting motion, whereas 다독이다 leans into the emotional follow-through of reassuring and steadying a person back together. Conjugation is the 이다-stem pattern: 토닥이- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 여, giving 토닥여 / 토닥여요, past 토닥였어요. It collocates with 등을/어깨를 토닥이다, 토닥여 주다, 위로하다, and 스스로를 토닥이다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 토닥이어요 — the stem-final ㅣ forces 여 → 토닥여요; and don't confuse the verb with the bare mimetic adverb 토닥토닥, even though they're family.

usage: 힘들어하는 친구를 다독여 줬어요.
I comforted and reassured my struggling friend.
다독이다 = comfort + steady someone emotionally; often with 주다.
스스로를 너무 다그치지 말고 다독여 주세요.
Don't push yourself too hard — be kind and reassure yourself.
Sets up the sharp contrast 다그치다 vs 다독이다.
팀원들을 다독여서 사기를 끌어올렸어요.
I rallied the team members and lifted morale.
다독이다 can mean to steady/encourage a whole group; 사기 = morale.
우는 동생을 다독이며 안아 줬어요.
I held my crying sibling, patting and reassuring them.
다독이며 = while comforting; -으며 links two simultaneous actions.
examples: 실패한 후배를 다독이며 다시 해 보라고 했어요.
I reassured the junior who'd failed and told them to try again.
다독이며 = while comforting; the -으며 connective overlaps the two acts.
엄마가 등을 다독여 주니까 마음이 놓였어요.
When Mom patted my back reassuringly, I felt at ease.
다독여 주다 + 마음이 놓이다 = to feel relieved.
팀원들을 다독여서 분위기를 다시 살렸어요.
I rallied the team members and revived the mood.
다독이다 can steady a group, not just one person; 분위기를 살리다 = revive the mood.
nuance: 다독이다 means to comfort and steady someone — gently patting while reassuring them so they settle, regroup, and feel supported. It is warmer and more emotionally loaded than the purely physical 토닥이다: where 토닥이다 highlights the literal pat-pat motion, 다독이다 carries the follow-through of 'pulling someone back together,' which is why it extends to rallying a group (팀을 다독여 분위기를 살리다) in a way 토닥이다 does not. Its true opposite is 다그치다 ('to press, push, urge harshly') — the same emotional axis pulled in reverse, which is why the pairing 다그치지 말고 다독여 주세요 ('don't pressure — reassure') is idiomatic. Conjugation is the 이다-stem pattern: 다독이- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 여, giving 다독여 / 다독여요, past 다독였어요. It collocates with 다독여 주다, 다독이며 (위로하다), 마음이 놓이다, and 사기를/분위기를 살리다. English-speaker pitfall: don't write 다독이어요 — the stem-final ㅣ forces 다독여요; and don't blur it with its near-opposite 다그치다, since mixing them up reverses your meaning entirely.

When the comfort is purely a physical pat, 토닥이다 fits better; reach for 다독이다 when you mean reassuring and steadying someone emotionally.

usage: 힘내라고 격려해 줬어요.
I encouraged them, saying 'hang in there.'
격려하다 + 주다 = encourage someone; slightly formal and warm.
서로 격려하면서 준비했어요.
We prepared while encouraging each other.
서로 격려하다 = mutual encouragement; common on teams.
사장님이 직원들을 격려하는 자리를 마련했어요.
The boss set up an occasion to encourage the staff.
격려하는 자리 = a morale-boosting gathering; formal register.
격려의 말씀 부탁드립니다.
We'd appreciate a few words of encouragement.
격려의 말(씀) = words of encouragement, a set noun phrase for events.
examples: 시험 떨어진 친구를 격려해 주고 싶었어요.
I wanted to encourage my friend who failed the exam.
Pairs with 떨어지다 (to fail); -아/어 주고 싶다 = want to do (for someone).
감독님이 선수들을 격려하는 연설을 했어요.
The coach gave a speech encouraging the players.
격려하다 is the go-to verb for pep talks and speeches.
힘든 시기에 격려해 주셔서 정말 감사했어요.
Thank you so much for encouraging me during a hard time.
Polite gratitude; very natural in messages to mentors and seniors.
nuance: 격려하다 is to encourage or cheer someone on with words — a pep talk, a 'you can do it,' a supportive note during a hard stretch. It is Sino-Korean: 激勵 combines 激 ('rouse, stir up') and 勵 ('urge on, exhort'), literally 'to stir up and spur on,' which is why it sounds a notch more formal and elevated than its native-feeling cousins. The dividing line versus 응원하다 (應援, 'to root for/cheer') is tone and setting: 응원하다 is energetic supporter-style cheering (a fan 응원s a team), while 격려하다 is more dignified, verbal encouragement, fitting speeches, workplaces, mentors, and 격려의 말씀 (words of encouragement) at formal events; and unlike the physical comforting of 다독이다 / 토닥이다, 격려하다 works through words. As a 하다-verb it conjugates regularly: 격려하- + 여 → 격려해 / 격려해요, past 격려했어요. It collocates with 격려해 주다, 서로 격려하다, 격려의 말씀, and 격려하는 연설. English-speaker pitfall: pronunciation — the ㄱ + ㄹ in 격려 nasalizes to [경녀] (romanized gyeongnyeo), so never say 'gyeok-lyeo'; and don't use 격려하다 for physically comforting someone — that's 다독이다 / 토닥이다.

격려하다 is encouragement through words; for physically comforting someone, use 다독이다 / 토닥이다 instead.

usage: 엄마한테 야단맞았어요.
I got told off by my mom.
Note the partner verb 야단맞다 = to get scolded (the receiving side); 한테 marks who from.
애를 너무 야단치지 마세요.
Don't scold the kid too harshly.
Gentle advice to a parent; 너무 = too (much).
선생님께 야단을 들었어요.
I got a scolding from the teacher.
야단(을) 듣다 = receive a scolding; shows the noun 야단 standing alone.
애들을 야단치기 전에 이유를 들어 보세요.
Before scolding the kids, hear them out first.
야단치기 전에 = before scolding; -기 전에 = before doing.
examples: 선생님이 떠든 학생들을 야단쳤어요.
The teacher scolded the students who were being noisy.
야단쳤어요 (past) = 야단치 + 었; the ㅣ + 어 fuses to 쳐.
거짓말한 걸 알고 부모님이 크게 야단치셨어요.
When they found out I lied, my parents scolded me a lot.
크게 야단치다 = to scold severely; -시- adds respect for the parents.
야단치기보다 차분히 타이르는 게 나아요.
It's better to gently reason with them than to scold.
Contrasts 야단치다 with 타이르다 (to admonish gently); -기보다 = rather than.
nuance: 야단치다 is to scold or tell someone off — a parent, teacher, or boss reprimanding a child or junior for doing wrong. It is built from the noun 야단 ('a fuss, an uproar, a scolding') plus 치다 ('to strike/deliver'), so it literally = 'to deliver a scolding,' which is why the noun can detach as 야단을 치다 and the receiving side surfaces as 야단을 듣다 / 야단을 맞다. It is stronger and more authority-driven than plain 화내다 (simply being angry): 야단치다 implies a power gap (older/senior reprimanding younger) and a corrective purpose, not just venting emotion. Its gentler neighbor is 타이르다 ('to admonish and reason with calmly'), which is why 야단치기보다 타이르다 ('reason rather than scold') is a natural contrast. Conjugation: 야단치- + 어 → the ㅣ+어 fuses to 쳐, giving 야단쳐 / 야단쳐요, past 야단쳤어요. It collocates with 크게 야단치다 (scold severely), 야단맞다/야단 듣다 (be scolded), and 혼나다 (get told off). English-speaker pitfall: 야단치다 is strictly the scolder's side — 'I got scolded' must be 야단맞았어요 or 혼났어요, never 야단쳤어요; and don't write 야단치어요, since ㅣ+어 fuses to 쳐.

It implies a senior-to-junior power gap; you don't 야단치다 your boss — between equals, 뭐라고 하다 or just 화내다 fits better.

usage: 내 꿈을 비웃지 마.
Don't sneer at my dream.
비웃다 takes a direct object (꿈을, 사람을) with 을/를; hurtful nuance.
사람들이 내 실수를 비웃었어요.
People laughed at my mistake mockingly.
Scornful laughter, not friendly laughter.
대놓고 비웃는 건 너무하잖아.
Openly sneering is going too far.
대놓고 비웃다 = sneer right to someone's face; 너무하다 = to be too much.
남을 비웃을 자격은 없어.
You have no right to sneer at others.
남을 비웃다 = mock others; 자격이 없다 = to have no right.
examples: 발음이 이상하다고 비웃을까 봐 말을 못 했어요.
I couldn't speak up, afraid they'd laugh at my pronunciation.
Very real fear for language learners; -을까 봐 = afraid that.
남을 비웃는 사람은 결국 신뢰를 잃어요.
People who sneer at others end up losing trust.
Moral-tone sentence; 남을 비웃다 = mock others.
콧방귀를 뀌며 내 계획을 비웃었어요.
He scoffed and sneered at my plan.
콧방귀를 뀌다 (to scoff through the nose) pairs idiomatically with 비웃다.
nuance: 비웃다 is to laugh at someone scornfully — to mock, sneer, ridicule, and look down on them. It is a compound of the prefix 비- (Sino-Korean 非/卑, carrying a 'belittling, disparaging' force, as in 비하 'to demean' or 비방 'to slander') plus the native verb 웃다 ('to laugh'), so it is literally 'belittling laughter,' which is exactly what separates it from neutral 웃다. The dividing line versus 놀리다 ('to tease') is intent and warmth: 놀리다 can be light, affectionate teasing between friends ('I'm just teasing you'), whereas 비웃다 is contemptuous and genuinely hurtful, with the laugher looking down on the target. It collocates with 남을/실수를/꿈을 비웃다, 대놓고 비웃다 (sneer openly), and the idiom 콧방귀를 뀌며 비웃다 (scoff and sneer). Conjugation point: 웃다 keeps its ㅅ — it is NOT a ㅅ-irregular — so the forms are 비웃어요 / 비웃었어요 / 비웃을 거예요, with the ㅅ intact. English-speaker pitfall: never drop that ㅅ (비웃어요, not 비웄어요); and don't use 비웃다 for friendly ribbing — that's 놀리다 — or you will sound far harsher and meaner than you intend.
